solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: We help lads working in better form

definitions.note: a phrase meaning in good shape, standing for an adjective

indicators.note: something working is set in motion and processed, so the letters are moved about

blocks.note: ten letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A trainer says that getting the boys to work has helped them get fitter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nicely proportioned and in good condition is in fine form, so the adjective matches the phrase.

clue.text: Long communications spies let loose

indicators.note: letters let loose are freed from their order and can fall anywhere

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Intelligence agents allow lengthy messages to slip out.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistles are formal letters, often lengthy, like those of the apostles in the New Testament.

clue.text: Slip out of jacket and cap

indicators.note: a jacket is the outer covering, so taking the word out of it strips its outside letters

blocks.note: to slip is to slide, here as a noun: a slide or slip

explanation.surface: Someone wriggles free of their coat and hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The jacket of SLIDE is its first and last letter; remove them and three letters remain.
explanation.definitionFit: A lid is a top or cover for a container, the same thing as a cap on a bottle or jar.

clue.text: Tried some cabbage with a dash of rosemary in it

indicators.note: a dash is a tiny amount, so only the first letter of the herb is used
in it says the small piece goes inside the vegetable word

blocks.note: cabbage is sold by the head
the first letter of the herb

explanation.surface: A cook sampled some cabbage seasoned with a little rosemary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tried' looks like tasted, fitting the kitchen scene, but here it is the legal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge who has heard a case has tried it in court, so the two past participles match.

clue.text: Hot? Tree will provide shade for you!

indicators.note: a tree shading something spreads over it, so the tree word wraps around

blocks.note: a tall tree
U sounds like you, as in text speak

explanation.surface: Feeling the heat? A tree will shade you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' looks like weather, but it is the slang sense of in demand.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hot is fashionable and much sought after, which is what a popular thing is.

clue.text: Old minister has ball holding power

indicators.note: holding means the dance word grips the other pieces within it

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance
standard abbreviation for old
abbreviation for minister or ministry

explanation.surface: A former government minister is holding a ball, presumably for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominance is control or supremacy over others, the state of having authority.

clue.text: Christmas in an English infirmary

blocks.note: first meaning: a mild exclamation of surprise, like 'Crikey'
second meaning: the initials of Great Ormond Street Hospital in London

explanation.surface: Spending the festive season in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: Great Ormond Street is a famous London children's hospital, known by its initials. 'Christmas!' is an old-fashioned expletive.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild oaths of astonishment, and the hospital's four initials spell the same word.

clue.text: Stupidly large towels one might hang on this?

indicators.note: doing something stupidly means doing it wrongly, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Big bath towels hung foolishly on a rail or peg.
explanation.definitionFit: The frame with a crossbar for executions is where a condemned person would be hanged.

clue.text: I was taken in as a baby?

definitions.text: I was taken in as a baby?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone recalls being adopted or fostered when very young
setter's reading: one who was fooled, and also an infant who suckles

explanation.definitionFit: A dupe who is easily fooled is called this, and the same word names a young animal still feeding at the teat.

clue.text: I’d primarily hold prawn crackers for music producer

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so only the opening letter is used
crackers means crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone at a Chinese takeaway says they'd hold prawn crackers back for a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Prawn crackers are a puffy snack, which is why the anagram signal hides so well.
explanation.definitionFit: An Aeolian instrument whose strings sound when the breeze blows across them makes music.

clue.text: Chap capturing official’s heart creates ill-will

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters are taken
capturing means seizing and holding, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the two central letters

explanation.surface: A man who wins over an officer's affections causes resentment.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is spite, the desire to harm someone, which is a form of hostility.

clue.text: Boss is charged by detective for dope

definitions.note: noun; the answer is used as a noun in 'Hey, stupid'

indicators.note: a thing charged is loaded or filled, so the first word is filled by the second

blocks.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud
private investigator

explanation.surface: A crime boss is arrested by a detective for drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' and 'charged' suggest crime and arrest; a boss here is an ornamental knob.
explanation.definitionFit: A dope is a fool, and the word can be used as an insulting noun for a slow-witted person too.

clue.text: Bit of meds gulped by a pale actor shakily?

definitions.text: Bit of meds gulped by a pale actor shakily?

indicators.note: a bit is a small part, so only the opening letter is taken
swallowed means taken inside, so one piece goes within the other
shaking things disturbs their order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter

explanation.surface: An unwell, wan actor nervously swallows some medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the picture of a performer taking a tablet.
explanation.definitionFit: This common painkiller, called acetaminophen in America, is a typical bit of medicine a pallid player might swallow.

clue.text: Solitary type embracing fellow city dweller

indicators.note: embracing means hugging around, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a person who keeps to themselves
a fellow of a university college is a don

explanation.surface: A recluse hugs another urbanite.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living in the British capital is a resident of that city, so a specific kind of urbanite.

clue.text: This stranger excited deep emotions

indicators.note: excited things are agitated and stirred up, so the letters move

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A mysterious newcomer stirred powerful feelings in someone.
explanation.definitionFit: One's strongest feelings of love or pity are said to be tugged when something moves one.

clue.text: Small and not very heavy, being thus?

definitions.text: Small and not very heavy, being thus?

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for small
the suffix -ish softens the word for weighing little

explanation.surface: A description of something that is fairly little and light.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer too: what is small and not very heavy is somewhat slight.
explanation.definitionFit: Slight means small or slender, and the -ish ending makes it 'rather slight', matching the clue's description.

clue.text: Popular release by old Republican author

blocks.note: in fashion
to vent is to let out
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A well-liked book launch by a former Republican writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author' suggests a novelist, but it means the originator of anything.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of a scheme or device is its creator, which is what someone who devises gadgets is.

clue.text: Trot supporting Labour

blocks.note: a trot is an old word for a toddler
bearing means holding up

explanation.surface: A Trotskyist backs the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Trot and Labour look political (a Trot is a Trotskyist); in fact Labour is giving birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour is the process of giving birth, and producing offspring is what the compound means.

clue.text: Report vagrant hanging around island

indicators.note: hanging around something means surrounding it, so one piece goes outside

blocks.note: a dosser is a British word for a homeless person sleeping rough
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A news story about a tramp loitering on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossier is a file of papers giving detailed information on a person or subject.

clue.text: Nursery’s selection of mediocre cherries

indicators.note: a selection is a run picked out, here a string taken straight from the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A garden nursery offers a range of poor-quality cherries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nursery' suggests a plant nursery to fit the fruit; it is a place for minding children.
explanation.definitionFit: A crèche is a day nursery where infants are looked after while parents work or shop.

clue.text: Trousers for dogs with dash of red lining

indicators.note: a dash is a small amount, so only the first letter is taken
a lining sits inside, so the small piece goes within the other word

blocks.note: female dogs
the first letter

explanation.surface: Pet clothing: trousers for dogs with a little red lining.
explanation.definitionFit: Britches is a variant spelling of breeches, short trousers fastened below the knee.

clue.text: Cop that gets under Jonathan’s skin

blocks.note: first meaning: an old British slang word for a policeman, after Sir Robert Peel
second meaning: a kitchen tool that removes the skin of fruit; Jonathan is a variety of apple

explanation.surface: A police officer who irritates a man called Jonathan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets under someone's skin' means annoys, but Jonathan is an apple here.
explanation.definitionFit: Peel founded London's police force, giving a nickname for officers, and the gadget literally removes the rind.

clue.text: Hit or stick

blocks.note: first meaning: to beat or thrash someone
second meaning: to glue something in place

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a choice between striking and staying, as in blackjack, but both words are verbs for the same answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a pasting is to thrash them, and to fix paper with glue is to apply adhesive.

clue.text: One’s about to eat side dish of seafood

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the first piece is read backwards
eating takes something inside, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: one is I, with 's as is shortened to S
a side or faction in a dispute

explanation.surface: Someone is about to eat a side dish of seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side dish' reads as one phrase, but side is wordplay and dish belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are langoustine tails, usually breaded and fried, served as a seafood meal.

clue.text: Lag back at 1am, after consuming drink endlessly

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter is dropped
consuming means taking in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: home at that hour means in, and late
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles home in the small hours after a heavy night's drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' looks like a prisoner or falling behind; here it is to wrap pipes against the cold.
explanation.definitionFit: To lag a boiler or pipes is to cover them with material that keeps heat in.

clue.text: Circuit record foremost of athletes breaks

indicators.note: foremost means first, so only the opening letter is kept
breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: a long-playing record
the first letter

explanation.surface: The leading runner breaks the track record.
explanation.walkthrough: Record looks like a best time, fitting athletics, but it is an LP disc.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing, each complete trip around the track or course is counted as one of these, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: Short beauty displays this kind of curve

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a belle is a beautiful woman

explanation.surface: A petite beauty shows off her curvy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Curve suggests a figure; it is the statistical graph of normal distribution.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell curve is the symmetrical hump-shaped graph of a normal distribution in statistics.

clue.text: Western or possibly Arabian music genre

blocks.note: an Arabian is one breed of the animal, and possibly signals an example
a form of musical drama

explanation.surface: A list of genres: Western, or maybe Arabian music.
explanation.walkthrough: Western and Arabian pose as rival musical styles; Western is a cowboy film.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse opera is slang for a cowboy film, a Western full of riders and gunfights.
